answer: The $500,000 joint limit on tax-free gain from selling a main home has not changed since it took effect in May 1997; in August 2026 prices that 1997 limit would be about $1,046,000. A couple who bought in 2000 crosses the limit when their gain (sale price minus purchase price and improvements) exceeds $500,000. If their home rose in value like its metro's price index from 2000 to 2026 Q2, that happens once the 2000 purchase price was above about $114,700 in Miami, $151,500 in Los Angeles, $164,500 in San Diego, $179,200 in Phoenix, $180,000 in Seattle, $212,200 in New York, $215,600 in Dallas, $226,400 in Boston, $227,700 in Denver, $254,400 in San Jose, $259,000 in San Francisco and $373,400 in Chicago (national index: $243,500; for a single seller with the $250,000 limit: $121,700). In 11 of these 12 metros the threshold is under $300,000 and in 5 it is under $200,000. Gain above the limit is taxed as a long-term capital gain on a sale, while heirs who inherit the home take a basis equal to its value at death.
guess: Long-time owners widely assume a married couple's home sale is tax-free because '$500,000 is more than our profit', and that the limit is something only expensive coastal homes ever reach.
changesDecision: In 11 of the 12 metros a 2000 purchase price under $300,000 is already enough for an index-typical gain to exceed the limit, including non-coastal metros such as Phoenix and Dallas, so the tax on the excess gain can become a real input in a sell-now-versus-keep decision that owners assume is tax-free. A viewer can check the threshold for their metro against their own purchase price plus improvements.

assumptions: Married couple filing jointly who meet the 2-out-of-5-year ownership and use tests; no prior exclusion used within 2 years.
Purchase during calendar year 2000 (average of the four 2000 quarters of the index); sale valued at 2026 Q2 index level.

The home's value moved exactly like its metro's FHFA all-transactions index; no capital improvements (which would raise basis and the threshold), no selling costs, no depreciation from business/rental use.
Metro = FHFA metropolitan division where one exists (e.g., Los Angeles-Long Beach-Glendale), otherwise the MSA.
Inflation comparison uses CPI-U (not seasonally adjusted) May 1997 to August 2026.
limits: History, not a forecast: index growth to 2026 Q2 says nothing about future prices. Metro indexes are averages; individual homes and neighborhoods diverge widely, and FHFA revises the index each quarter. Thresholds ignore improvements and selling costs, which reduce the gain. The episode measures exposure to the limit; it does not compute any viewer's tax or recommend selling or holding. Not personal advice.
